title: Scenario 2: Engagement

support.label: Hints on request
support.description: No walkthrough this time. Hints unlock after your first flag or two minutes on the dashboard, and hint use is recorded. Not every chart has a problem.

briefing.from: Marcus Lee, Head of Digital Marketing, JT Morgan
briefing.subject: Engagement is growing. Can we double the FlexBuy budget?
body: FlexBuy has been live for 12 weeks. Our dashboard shows the repeat-plan rate climbing steadily, and plans per active user were very strong in the first weeks.
I'd like to double the FlexBuy marketing budget next quarter to accelerate this momentum.
Before I take this to the VP, can you confirm that engagement is really growing and that this is the right move?

metrics.name: Repeat-plan rate: first-time users who open a second plan within 90 days
metrics.feedback: The core engagement measure. It has a defined cohort (first-time users) and a defined window (90 days), so it can be compared across weeks and segments.

metrics.name: Autopay enrollment rate among new plans
metrics.feedback: Autopay signals a customer intends to keep using the product, and it reduces missed payments. It is a rate with a clear denominator.

metrics.name: Share of FlexBuy users with a plan in the last 30 days
metrics.feedback: An activity rate: of everyone who has used FlexBuy, how many are still using it. It separates ongoing engagement from one-time trial.

metrics.name: Median days between a customer's first and second plan
metrics.feedback: Time to repeat. Shorter is better, and it is anchored to clear events, so it is comparable across cohorts.

metrics.name: Service contacts per 1,000 plans
metrics.feedback: A guardrail normalized by volume. Rising contacts per plan mean customers are confused or having problems as usage grows.

metrics.name: Customers who turn FlexBuy off in settings, per 1,000 users
metrics.feedback: A guardrail for annoyance: customers actively opting out of the feature. It must not rise as engagement efforts increase.

metrics.name: Plans cancelled after the first installment
metrics.feedback: A guardrail for regret. If customers cancel once they see the first payment, the engagement is not healthy.

metrics.name: Total plans since launch
metrics.feedback: A cumulative count that can only rise. It cannot show whether customers are coming back more or less often.

metrics.name: Average time spent on the FlexBuy screen
metrics.feedback: More time on a screen can mean confusion as easily as interest. It does not tell you whether customers return to use the product.

metrics.name: Taps on the FlexBuy button
metrics.feedback: Taps measure curiosity or accidental clicks, not repeat use of the product.

metrics.name: Total registered FlexBuy users
metrics.feedback: Registration is a one-time event. A large user count says nothing about whether those users are still engaged.

metrics.name: Open rate of FlexBuy marketing emails
metrics.feedback: This measures response to marketing, not engagement with the product itself.

segment_note: Existing cardholders already had a JT Morgan credit card before using FlexBuy.

hints.s2_simpson: A total can move in the opposite direction from every group inside it. Try the segment filter on the repeat-plan chart.
hints.s2_novelty: Is week 1 a fair baseline? Look at when plans per active user stops changing.
hints.s2_threshold: If the $500 boundary did not matter, how many purchases would you expect just above it compared with just below it?

decision.question: Should marketing double the FlexBuy budget next quarter?

ship.feedback: The 'growing engagement' headline is a Simpson's paradox: repeat use is falling in both segments, and the total rises only because the customer mix shifted. Doubling spend would buy more customers whose repeat use is declining.

iterate.feedback: This matches the expert view. Hold the budget increase, find out why repeat use is falling within each segment, and test the fee design that customers are clearly working around.

rollback.feedback: Too far. Engagement is weakening, but the feature still has steady usage and autopay enrollment is rising. Nothing here justifies pulling FlexBuy.

evidence.text: Within both customer segments, the repeat-plan rate declined over the 12 weeks.
The customer mix shifted toward existing cardholders, who repeat more.
About three times as many purchases fall just below $500 as just above it.
Plans per active user in weeks 1 to 3 were a launch spike; it has been flat since week 5.
Autopay enrollment rose from about 34% to about 53% of new plans.
The overall repeat-plan rate rose from about 25% to about 28%.
evidence.why: This is the misleading headline: it rises only because the customer mix changed, while both segments decline.

evidence.text: Week 1 had the highest plans per active user of the quarter.
evidence.why: That was a launch spike. Comparing against it makes every later week look like a decline, or an early peak to recapture.

decision.expert_rationale: Iterate, and hold the budget increase. The claim that engagement is growing is a Simpson's paradox: the blended repeat-plan rate rose from about 25% to 28% only because the customer mix shifted toward existing cardholders, who repeat more. Within both segments, repeat use fell, from about 40% to 34% for existing cardholders and from about 19% to 14% for customers new to JT Morgan credit. Doubling marketing would mainly add customers whose repeat use is declining. The very high plans per active user in weeks 1 to 3 was a launch spike; the steady state is about 1.15 and flat. Autopay enrollment rising from about 34% to 53% is a genuine positive. Separately, roughly three times as many purchases fall between $450 and $499.99 as between $500 and $549.99, so customers are working around the 4.5% FlexBuy Plus fee; I would test a lower or tiered fee before scaling. Next steps: report repeat rates by segment, investigate why repeat use is falling, and revisit the budget once the within-segment repeat rate has been stable for four consecutive weeks.

objectives: Define a repeat-use rate with a proper cohort and window (Apply).
Detect segment reversals, launch spikes, and threshold effects (Analyze).
Decide whether the evidence supports more spend (Evaluate).
why_it_matters: Budgets are often doubled on a total that looks healthy while every customer group underneath it is declining. Segmenting before concluding protects that money.

first_impression.question: Before you analyze anything: based on the memo alone, how is the launch going?

options.mixed: Mixed: some parts work, some do not

expert_short: Going worse than it looks. Repeat use is falling in every segment; the overall rise is a mix shift. Autopay is a genuine positive, and the fee threshold is shaping behavior.

retrieval.q: A rate falls in the same week the eligible population doubles. What do you check first?
options: Whether the app had an outage
retrieval.why: A change in who is counted can move a rate even when behavior is unchanged (Scenario 1).

retrieval.q: Which of these is a guardrail rather than a success metric?
retrieval.why: Opt-outs must not get worse while you grow adoption. Impressions are vanity; creation rate is success.

define_it.intent: Of customers who tried FlexBuy, how many come back for another plan?

num.label: Numerator: what you count
num.correct: Customers who opened a second plan within 90 days

options.Customers who opened a second plan withi: Right: it counts returning customers once each.
options.Total plans opened: Total plans grows with new customers too, so it cannot isolate coming back.
options.App logins: Logging in is not the same as using FlexBuy again.

den.label: Denominator: who could have done it
den.correct: Customers whose first plan was at least 90 days ago

options.Customers whose first plan was at least: Right: everyone in this group has had the full 90 days to come back.
options.All registered FlexBuy users: Recent customers have not had 90 days yet, so the rate would look worse during fast growth.
options.Total plans opened: Plans, not customers: the units do not match the numerator.

win.label: Time window
win.correct: Within 90 days of the first plan

options.Within 90 days of the first plan: Right: a fixed window makes cohorts comparable.
options.Any time since launch: Early customers have had longer to return, so older cohorts would always look better.

define_it.guardrail_prompt: Name one guardrail you would watch alongside repeat use, and say why.
model_guardrails: Service contacts per 1,000 plans: more usage should not mean more confused customers.
Customers who turn FlexBuy off, per 1,000 users: a sign engagement efforts are annoying people.
Plans cancelled after the first installment: regret once the first payment arrives.

exemplars: Level 1: "Engagement is up, so double the budget." (one factor, the headline)
Level 2: "The overall repeat rate rose, both segments fell, autopay rose, and purchases cluster under $500." (several facts, not connected)

Level 3: "Iterate. The overall rise is a mix shift; repeat use fell in both segments, so more spend would buy declining engagement. Customers avoid the fee at $500, so test the fee design." (connected reasoning)
Level 4: Level 3, plus "Revisit the budget once within-segment repeat rates hold steady for four weeks, and report repeat use by segment." (a decision rule that reaches beyond this case)
